case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old woman was evaluated for generalized dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, severe scoliosis, and motor development disorder that began in her childhood. Born by cesarean delivery to nonconsanguineous parents, she developed difficulties with head control, standing, and feeding at age 10 months. Subsequently, she faced progressive motor challenges (walking, speech, and swallow); contractures in her fingers, toes, wrists, and knees; and scoliosis. In adolescence, she experienced progressive stiffness, episodes of painful spasms and oculomotor crisis, and galactorrhea unrelated to childbirth in adulthood. Her symptoms worsened with age and progressed to her using a wheelchair, having difficulty in speech, and not having access to education. She had a younger brother with similar symptoms who passed away at age 20 years of unknown causes. Upon presentation at age 31 years, she was admitted to our center for further evaluation. She had thin limbs and was of standard height. The neurological and psychological examinations revealed scoliosis, contractures in her fingers and toes, carpal inversion, dysarthria, dysphagia, hypertonia, decreased tendon reflexes, absence of Babinski sign (Figure, A and B), and no psychiatric problems. Blood test results indicated hyperprolactinemia (prolactin level of 47.40 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1). An electroencephalogram revealed atypical spike-slow wave synchronization in specific brain regions during sleep. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed significant global atrophy particularly in her anterior temporal, lateral, and frontal regions (Figure, C). Levodopa treatment was initiated but quickly resulted in drug-induced hyperkinesia (Video).
case_info.caption: A, Characteristic features of hypertonia. A 31-year-old woman with flexion contracture of the fingers and carpal inversion. B, Severe scoliosis. C, Brain magnetic resonance imaging showing prominent atrophy in the anterior, lateral temporal, and frontal regions.
case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

[Role]
You are a senior clinician (the Doctor) trying to make a clinical decision about the given patient case.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.


[Information Sparsity]
You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.


[Current Context]
- You have examined the patient case.
- Form your own clinical judgment.

[Task]
Based on the case below, state your initial decision and reasoning.

[Expression Style]
- Keep your response under 5 sentences.
- Focus on clinical evidence.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your opening message stating your initial decision and reasoning -- this is
    the only field the AI partner sees",
  "belief": "the clinical decision you have independently made",
  "confidence": "a number between 0 and 1 for how confident you are in that belief (0 = no
    confidence at all, 1 = completely certain) -- your own internal state, not shown to the AI",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why (your terse internal justification,
    separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Cerebral palsy
  B. Hereditary spastic paraplegia
  C. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism
  D. Tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency

[Instruction]
State your independent clinical decision and reasoning. Start the conversation.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side

- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).

Born by cesarean delivery to nonconsanguineous parents, she developed difficulties with head control, standing, and feeding at age 10 months. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed significant global atrophy particularly in her anterior temporal, lateral, and frontal regions (Figure, C). case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old woman was evaluated for generalized dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, severe scoliosis, and motor development disorder that began in her childhood. Born by cesarean delivery to nonconsanguineous parents, she developed difficulties with head control, standing, and feeding at age 10 months. Subsequently, she faced progressive motor challenges (walking, speech, and swallow); contractures in her fingers, toes, wrists, and knees; and scoliosis. In adolescence, she experienced progressive stiffness, episodes of painful spasms and oculomotor crisis, and galactorrhea unrelated to childbirth in adulthood. Her symptoms worsened with age and progressed to her using a wheelchair, having difficulty in speech, and not having access to education. She had a younger brother with similar symptoms who passed away at age 20 years of unknown causes. Upon presentation at age 31 years, she was admitted to our center for further evaluation. She had thin limbs and was of standard height. The neurological and psychological examinations revealed scoliosis, contractures in her fingers and toes, carpal inversion, dysarthria, dysphagia, hypertonia, decreased tendon reflexes, absence of Babinski sign (Figure, A and B), and no psychiatric problems. Blood test results indicated hyperprolactinemia (prolactin level of 47.40 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1). An electroencephalogram revealed atypical spike-slow wave synchronization in specific brain regions during sleep. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed significant global atrophy particularly in her anterior temporal, lateral, and frontal regions (Figure, C). Levodopa treatment was initiated but quickly resulted in drug-induced hyperkinesia (Video).
case_info.caption: A, Characteristic features of hypertonia. A 31-year-old woman with flexion contracture of the fingers and carpal inversion. B, Severe scoliosis. C, Brain magnetic resonance imaging showing prominent atrophy in the anterior, lateral temporal, and frontal regions.
case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.
